transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-11 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alice Morgan (Redwood AE), Devon Park (Redwood SE), Markus Chen (BlueWave - Platform), Priya Singh (BlueWave - ML Infra), Rafael Ortiz (BlueWave - CTO)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive on multi-region routing and failover. Goals: align on routing policy options (latency-first, cost-aware, capacity-weighted), discuss KV cache implications for cold start vs warm failovers, understand VPC/on-prem constraints, and agree next steps for bench and DR tabletop.

Topics covered:
- routing policy primitives (latency, cost, capacity, weighted failover)
- cold failover vs gradual draining and cache warming
- quantization/model variant implications across regions
- VPC peering and private deployment considerations (BlueWave internal regs)
- runbook & DR playbook outline and test plan

Transcript:
00:00:00 Alice: ok everyone thanks for joining, we're gonna run through the multi region routing and the DR playbook today, just to sync on options and any blockers on your side
00:00:08 Rafael: yep, thanks Alice. We've got Markus and Priya on the line. Want to make sure latency for EU customers stays under 120ms p95 even during failover, that's the big ask from product
00:00:20 Alice: totally understood. We'll talk SLA approaches and fallback. Devon, wanna kick off with the routing model options?
00:00:26 Devon: yeah sure. So at a high level we usually think about three policies: latency-first (route to lowest RTT region), capacity-aware (route by available dedicated pool capacity), and cost-weighted (prefer cheaper regions unless latency would violate SLO). You can also do hybrid policies like latency with cost thresholding.
00:00:50 Markus: quick question — how sticky is the KV cache across region switches? if we route a session to EU1 then fail to US1, will the KV cache be usable?
00:01:01 Devon: great question. Short answer: not automatically. KV cache is per-region and often per-serving cluster. We support a couple patterns: replicate KV entries asynchronously to warm targets (expensive at scale), or warm on-demand using a prefix-level replay, or accept a cold-cache penalty and rely on smaller model fallbacks to keep latency.
00:01:26 Priya: replicate seems risky for us because of EU data residency rules; asynchronous replication might violate residency unless we scrub identified data. Is there a hybrid approach?
00:01:36 Devon: yes, you can selectively replicate only non-PII cache keys, or maintain a metadata-only index that speeds up warm-up without moving payloads. Another approach is pre-provisioning model instances in a standby region with kept KV snapshot on encrypted storage accessible inside EU boundaries.
00:01:58 Rafael: I also want to understand the sequence during an outage. Like, do you do instant failover to another region or do you shift traffic gradually? Our concerns are cache thrash and request error spikes.
00:02:12 Alice: our recommended default is staged failover: circuit-breaker triggers then traffic shifts to a nearby region with ramped traffic (e.g., 10% -> 30% -> 100% over a few minutes) while we monitor error rates and latency. For critical SLAs we can configure active-active with session affinity to reduce cold-cache impact, but that requires cross-region replication work.
00:02:32 Devon: to add — we use a short-lived sticky token to prefer region affinity. On failover the token expires and clients reconnect; that gives you a predictable window to warm caches. We also have heuristics to pin model variants so quantized models only run in regions where the proper GPU kernels exist.
00:02:50 Markus: about quantized models — is it true that a 4-bit quantized variant can have different throughput characteristics across regions depending on runtime kernels? we saw odd perf on our edge cluster before.
00:03:01 Devon: yes, exactly. Quantization interacts with the serving runtime and hardware. Some regions have newer GPUs or optimized kernels, so the same quantized model might be faster in us-west than in eu-north due to kernel availability. That's why our routing policy can be model-aware — you can route model variant X to region A and variant Y to region B.
00:03:21 Priya: that helps. For compliance, can we restrict which model variants are allowed in EU? e.g., disallow models that were trained on external data that we can't host in EU?
00:03:31 Alice: yes, on the platform you can pin model versions per-tenant/region and enforce a policy that blocks non-EU-validated variants from spinning up in EU zones. We'll include the example config in the playbook.
00:03:44 Rafael: stepping back, we need to see numbers — latency delta when KV cache is cold, plus the cost delta for active-active replication. Can you run a bench sim?
00:03:54 Devon: absolutely. We'll simulate warm vs cold, with steady qps and spike scenarios. We'll include continuous batching effects — in some cases batching actually *reduces* tail latency at high qps because tokens amortize. But at low qps, batching introduces extra wait so it's a parameter to tune per-region.
00:04:16 Markus: about batching — does Redwood do adaptive batching based on observed inter-arrival times? we don't want fixed batch windows.
00:04:23 Devon: yeah, the runtime uses continuous batching with a small max wait (configurable). It will flush early if latency budget is tight. You can set per-route latency SLOs so the batching aggressiveness adapts by route.
00:04:35 Priya: ok. On VPC/on-prem: we'd like private deployment in EU for certain regulated accounts. How does multi-region routing work with a mix of private EU and hosted US?
00:04:46 Alice: good point. We support split control plane: you can have a private control plane in your VPC in EU that registers to Redwood's global routing mesh. For routing, we treat private clusters as first-class endpoints and you can set a policy to prefer private endpoints for EU tenant traffic. Failover to hosted endpoints is optional and must be explicitly enabled — many customers disable cross-boundary failover for regulatory reasons.
00:05:07 Rafael: so if we disable cross-boundary failover, we still need a local DR plan inside EU — like a hot-standby in a second EU region?
00:05:15 Alice: yes. For full DR inside the region you want at least two AZs or two regions within EU with replication options. We'll show a template: primary EU1 active, EU2 standby with pre-warmed models and KV snapshot refreshed every N minutes. If cross-boundary failover is off, the playbook calls for human-in-the-loop escalation to approve temporary cross-boundary route if absolutely necessary.
00:05:36 Devon: also note the impact on token-level cost attribution when you failover — cost buckets shift to the region that runs inference. We'll include a cost model spreadsheet for you to run scenarios.
00:05:47 Markus: great. On the tech side, what about DNS vs agent-based routing? we use a mix of ELBs and internal proxies. How granular can Redwood's routing be?
00:05:58 Devon: we support multiple routing ingress options: DNS-based with low TTLs for coarse shifts, proxy-level routing for per-request decisions (preferred for low-latency SLOs), and an edge agent that can perform local affinity. For per-request policy you usually front with an internal proxy that attaches metadata so Redwood can make decisions on request attributes, model, tenant, compliance flags, etc.
00:06:20 Priya: do you have examples of circuit-breaker thresholds or canaries? we want recommended numbers not just theory
00:06:27 Alice: yes, in the draft playbook we'll include suggested thresholds — for example: p95 latency increase > 30% for 3 consecutive minutes triggers a canary cutback; error rate > 2% triggers a partial rollback; on failover ramp: 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% each minute with automated health checks. Those are starting points and should be tuned to your traffic shape.
00:06:49 Rafael: sounds reasonable. Can the platform do automated rollback to previous model versions if quality regressions are detected during a failover?
00:06:56 Devon: we have model rollouts that support automatic rollback based on perf and quality hooks. If you wire up our evals/metrics, a metric like BLEU or custom scoring can trigger a rollback and route traffic back. For production safety we recommend a canary and A/B gating before full cutover.
00:07:12 Markus: quick nit — if we ramp to a region with different quantization, are we risking output drift that could violate product expectations? how do customers handle consistency?
00:07:23 Devon: two patterns: 1) enforce model parity (same exact weights and quantization) across regions — pain to maintain but deterministic, or 2) allow variant parity but monitor for drift via example-based evals during failover. We often recommend hybrid: critical intents use pinned parity models; lower-risk routes use region-specific optimized variants.
00:07:44 Priya: ok. Anything about KV cache expiring keys causing policy issues? we have long-tail sessions where losing KV state is user-visible.
00:07:53 Devon: for long-tail sessions you can do session replication: store session state in an encrypted cross-region datastore (not the per-region in-memory KV) and use an index to lazily hydrate the in-memory KV on the standby. That keeps payloads resident without full eager replication. It does add read latency on first miss though.
00:08:13 Rafael: what's the estimated cold-penalty we should plan for? like median increase in latency if KV is cold and we fallback to smaller model?
00:08:22 Devon: rough numbers: warm-cache p95 90–120ms depending on model; cold-cache fallback to smaller model might bring p95 back to 150–250ms. If no fallback, cold-cache with full model could spike to 400–800ms for big models. We'll provide specific numbers from bench.
00:08:40 Markus: that range is wide. please give us a bench with our 512-token distribution and our avg qps of 60.
00:08:48 Devon: noted. We'll use your token distribution. We'll also include batch-size sensitivity sweeps.
00:08:55 Alice: operationally, playbook wise we propose sections: detection, automated mitigation (circuit breaker & ramp), manual escalation, forensics & postmortem, and customer comms templates. We'll add runbook snippets and a checklist for VPC peering and private control plane failover.
00:09:12 Priya: what about audit logs for cross-region routing decisions? we need a trail that shows where traffic was routed and why (policy triggered).
00:09:19 Devon: yes we log routing decisions with metadata: timestamp, request id, tenant id, chosen region, decision reason (latency, capacity, manual). Logs are exportable to your SIEM and available in the Console for 90 days by default (retention add-on available).
00:09:34 Rafael: security question: does the KV cache or standby snapshot ever leave the customer's VPC unencrypted?
00:09:40 Alice: snapshots are encrypted at rest and in transit. For private deploys we can ensure snapshots stay inside your VPC; for hosted failover replication we'd need explicit agreement because data will cross boundaries. We'll put options in the playbook and mark them with compliance risk levels.
00:09:56 Markus: ok great. Can we simulate an AZ gone scenario first, then a full region failover? we'd like to ramp up the tests in complexity
00:10:04 Devon: yep recommended approach: AZ failover -> regional AZ degradation -> full region failover -> cross-boundary emergency failover. Each test has checklists and expected metrics. We'll provide sample SLO gates for each stage.
00:10:17 Rafael: any gotchas for private on-prem nodes? we have an air-gapped environment for some clients.
00:10:24 Devon: air-gapped means you can't do automatic cross-region routing; the control plane can be configured to accept only telemetry and health pings through an approved channel. Failover must be orchestrated by ops in that case — our runbook includes manual steps and scripts to bring standby up from local snapshots.
00:10:38 Priya: we'll definitely want a tabletop exercise. can you draft the scenario and expected roles?
00:10:44 Alice: yes, that'll be part of the runbook deliverable. We'll propose roles: BlueWave on-call, BlueWave SRE lead, Redwood SE, Redwood Ops, product comms. We'll include timelines for each play.
00:10:56 Markus: last thing — what's the onboarding friction for the private control plane? manpower, certs, time to first test?
00:11:03 Alice: typical timeline: private control plane in VPC takes 2–4 weeks depending on networking approvals, VPC peering or transit setup, and KMS onboarding. On-prem air-gap takes longer ~4–8 weeks. We'll provide a checklist to speed approvals.
00:11:16 Rafael: good, thanks. let's recap next steps
00:11:20 Alice: recap: 1) Devon to run multi-region bench with your token distribution and deliver results 2) Alice will share the draft playbook and VPC checklist 3) Markus sends latency histograms and qps profile 4) Priya confirms residency constraints. We'll target getting the bench and docs to you mid next week.
00:11:37 Priya: thanks everyone
00:11:39 Rafael: thanks, bye
